stem: After administering a hazardous antineoplastic drug, the nurse removes a disposable gown and chemotherapy gloves that are contaminated with the drug. How should these items be discarded?

options.A: Place them in the facility's designated hazardous-drug waste container according to hazardous-drug disposal procedures
options.B: Place them in regular trash because they are disposable PPE rather than medication
options.C: Place them in an ordinary sharps container even though they contain no sharps
options.D: Rinse the disposable PPE in the sink before placing it in regular waste

rationale: OSHA hazardous-drug guidance identifies used gloves, gowns, and related disposable materials contaminated with hazardous drugs as hazardous-drug-related waste and recommends designated, labeled hazardous-drug waste bags and covered containers. Such contaminated PPE should not be placed in ordinary trash, an unrelated sharps container, or rinsed in a sink. Exact disposal requirements must also follow applicable federal, state, local, and facility rules. Therefore A is the best answer.
educational_objective: Dispose of disposable PPE contaminated with hazardous antineoplastic drugs in the designated hazardous-drug waste stream according to facility and applicable regulatory procedures.
source_organization: U.S. Department of Labor — Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
source_document_title: Hospitals eTool — Pharmacy: Disposal of Hazardous Drugs
source_locator: Recognized Controls and Work Practices — Hazardous waste containers and disposal: use thick leak-proof plastic bags for discarded gloves, gowns and other related disposable material; clearly label bags as hazardous-drug-related waste; keep the bag in a covered container labeled for hazardous-drug waste; dispose according to applicable federal, state and local regulations
source_claim_supported: Disposable PPE contaminated with hazardous drugs should enter a designated, labeled hazardous-drug waste stream rather than ordinary trash, with final disposal following applicable regulations and facility procedures.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — Handling Hazardous and Infectious Materials, printed p.25 / PDF p.29: follow procedures for handling biohazardous and hazardous materials; demonstrate safe handling techniques
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hazardous-drug contaminated waste disposal
correction_summary: Narrowed the source item from a broad statement about all contaminated materials and IV tubing to a directly supported scenario involving contaminated disposable PPE. Added the required regulatory/facility-procedure nuance and removed the implication that one disposal category universally covers every type or quantity of hazardous-drug waste.
audit_findings: A is directly supported by current OSHA hazardous-drug disposal guidance. B places contaminated PPE in ordinary waste, C misuses a sharps container for non-sharps, and D creates an unnecessary contamination route. The item deliberately avoids classifying residual-drug tubing, bulk versus trace waste, or RCRA hazardous waste because those classifications depend on specific contents and applicable regulations. NCSBN 2026 mapping is explicit. Independent second pass found one best answer and no unresolved conflict.
